sentences.text: The animal belongs to the genus Sauroposeidon, a name derived from Greek words for 'lizard' and 'Poseidon,' the sea god.
The original fossil find consisted of four connected mid-neck vertebrae along with their attached ribs.
These neck bones were extremely thin and filled with tiny air cells, similar to chicken or ostrich bones, to reduce weight.
Its largest neck vertebra measures 1.4 meters in length, which is the longest sauropod neck vertebra ever recorded.
Extrapolations suggest the animal's head could reach a height of 16.5 to 18 meters, making it one of the tallest known dinosaurs.
Estimates suggest the animal reached lengths of 27 to 34 meters and masses of 40 to 60 metric tons.
Until 2006, Sauroposeidon was likely the tallest dinosaur ever unearthed, though it was neither the longest nor the heaviest.
The first fossils were four neck vertebrae found in rural Oklahoma dating to about 110 million years ago.
When discovered in 1994, the remains were mistakenly identified as petrified wood due to their size and age.
Juveniles were likely preyed upon by apex predators such as Acrocanthosaurus atokensis and Deinonychus antirrhopus, while adults had few natural predators.
The genus Sauroposeidon was named by Wedel et al. in 2000.
Sauroposeidon was initially considered to be closely related to Brachiosaurus and Giraffatitan, both members of the family Brachiosauridae.
The fossils date from the Early Cretaceous, specifically between 113 and 110 million years ago.
It lived on the shores of the ancient Gulf of Mexico in a vast river delta environment similar to the modern Mississippi delta.
It is debated whether the animal is closely related to Brachiosaurus, which could make size estimates inaccurate.
There are differences between some specimens, but they cannot be confidently distinguished from each other.
Researchers debate whether the mass estimate is too high, suggesting the rest of its body might have been as slender as its neck.
